idea.body: Two patterns come up so often that it pays to recognize them on sight. A difference of squares, a^2 - b^2, always factors as (a - b)(a + b). For example, x^2 - 9 factors as (x - 3)(x + 3), since 9 is 3 squared. A perfect square trinomial, a^2 + 2ab + b^2 or a^2 - 2ab + b^2, always factors as (a + b)^2 or (a - b)^2. For example, x^2 + 6x + 9 factors as (x + 3)^2. The first and last terms are squares, and the middle term is twice their product. Spotting these two patterns saves the trial and error that ordinary trinomials need. Always check by expanding the factors back out.

figure.alt: An area model for (x - 3)(x + 3), with the two middle parts cancelling.

workedExample.prompt: Factor x^2 - 25 using the difference of squares pattern.
steps: x^2 - 25 is a square, x^2, minus another square, 25.
25 is 5 squared, so this matches a^2 - b^2 with a = x and b = 5.
A difference of squares a^2 - b^2 factors as (a - b)(a + b).

figure.alt: An area model for (x - 5)(x + 5), with the two middle parts cancelling.

ways.name: Spot the pattern
ways.when: Use this first whenever the expression could be a difference of squares or a perfect square.
steps: x^2 and 16 are both perfect squares: x^2 and 4^2.
A difference of squares a^2 - b^2 factors as (a - b)(a + b).
Here a = x and b = 4, so x^2 - 16 factors as (x - 4)(x + 4).
ways.trap: Trying to factor a sum of squares like x^2 + 16, which never factors this way.

figure.alt: An area model for (x - 4)(x + 4), with the two middle parts cancelling.

frames.caption: x^2 and 16 are both perfect squares.
A difference of squares factors as (a-b)(a+b).

ways.name: Fall back to the general method
ways.when: Use this if you are not sure the special pattern applies.
steps: Find two numbers that multiply to -36 and add to 0: 6 and -6.
This matches the difference of squares pattern, confirming the shortcut.
ways.trap: Forgetting the middle term is 0 and searching for numbers that add to something else.

ways.name: Test with the doubling check
ways.when: Use this before factoring a trinomial, to confirm it truly is a perfect square.
steps: Take the square root of the first and last terms of x^2 + 14x + 49: x and 7.
Double their product: 2 times x times 7 is 14x.
14x matches the middle term, so this is a perfect square trinomial.
ways.trap: Skipping the doubling check and assuming any trinomial with square outer terms is a perfect square.
